primaries.primaryEn: Though one-formed, She who shines in split forms — in the world's birth, keeping and ending; who turns as the never-fallen Lord's power — that Brahman-power, I stretch toward. (Verse 1, Harikṛṣṇa's opening.) In simple words the poet bows first: one Mother, many shining faces — in making, keeping and ending the world — turning as the faultless Lord's own power; that power of Brahman I reach for.

The holy four-armed nectar-bodied Caṇḍikā's true story is told apart — so may the company of the wise be pleased here, since even a parrot's song delights the good. (Verse 2.) In simple words the poet's humble wish: I now tell apart the true story of four-armed nectar-bodied Caṇḍikā — may wise readers be pleased, for the good delight even in a parrot's sweet chatter.

Long ago, Vedavyāsa's pupil Jaimini — doubting among Mahābhārata matters about spirit-stuff — reached sage Mārkaṇḍeya and spoke. (Frame opening, with old note.) Combined with the old note: but 'this is no tale-hour for us,' said the sage, so directed him — 'ask the four birds on Vindhya hill, knowers of every meaning.' And he did so. Then, to oblige Jaimini's questions, while explaining creation and the Purāṇa-limbs, the religion-birds, keen to teach the fourth Purāṇa-limb, follow the Mārkaṇḍeya-Bhāguri dialogue-tale, opening the eighth Manu-age, and said: 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks.' Mārkaṇḍeya means Mṛkaṇḍu's son, a man (Mṛkaṇḍu — like a deer, tearing by self-yoga; tearing deer, or deer-itchy — grammar debated; his son is Mārkaṇḍeya). And starting the book with the long-lived one is for blessing. (Verse 1.) In simple words the story-frame: doubting Jaimini came to Mārkaṇḍeya, who sent him to the four wonder-birds of Vindhya; and those dharma-birds begin the eighth Manu-age tale with 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks' — Mṛkaṇḍu's long-lived son, named auspiciously at the start.

'To whom Brahmā, to whom Hari, to whom Rudra made salutation — to Her, salutation, salutation, salutation again and again.' (Verse 1, Śāntanava's opening.) In simple words the second opener bows: Brahmā bows to whom, Viṣṇu bows to whom, Rudra bows to whom — to Her, again and again salutation.

Cows fallen in a dark well of untaught mouths pain the sage — those, drive forth on every side, eager each for its own calf and good. Drawn hard by Pāṇini-gathered ropes, may praises become wish-cows, hating darkness-heaps, bright-shining. (Verse 2.) In simple words a poet's riddle-prayer: Vedic hymns fallen into a dark well of unlearned mouths grieve the sage — pull them out all around with Pāṇini's rope-rules, each eager for its sense-calf, till praises turn wish-cows, darkness-hating, bright.

Meditated with Aiṃ-Hrīṃ-Śrī words — this world, to make, to guard — at dissolving time, able, compassion-formed, Brahmā's Fortune, Caṇḍikā. (Verse 3, with old note.) Combined with the old note: having worshipped the first power, misery-burning, holy Tomara — Śāntanu, famed in Mārkaṇḍeya-Purāṇa glory — explains for fame. (Verse 3.) In simple words: the world pondered with seed-words Aiṃ-Hrīṃ-Śrī — to make, to guard — and at melting time, able, mercy-formed Brahmā-Fortune Caṇḍikā; and the Tomara-line sage Śāntanu, famed in Purāṇa glory, explains Her to spread Her fame.

The Mārkaṇḍeya-told wonderful Goddess-greatness — few-lettered, endless-sensed, face-averted from wrong readings. (Verse 1, Harikṛṣṇa on the book.) In simple words the book's praise: Mārkaṇḍeya's wonderful Goddess-glory — short in letters, endless in sense, turning its face from bad readings.

Lucky-youth Śāntanu, fame-heaped, Tomara-born — explains, beating back bad-explaining traditions. (Verse 5.) In simple words the author signs: lucky young Śāntanu of fame-heap, Tomara-born, explains — pushing aside the whole line of bad explainers.

Om, salutation to Caṇḍikā. 'She guards (avati) the worshipper from this (world); She guards Brahman too' — so analysed; 'ava' in guarding-sense. (Mantra grammar, with old note.) Combined with the old note: the affix-rules, vowel-changes and indeclinable Om explained letter by letter — Om means assent, and stands first at every beginning; Om the one-letter Brahman, overlord of all mantras; 'salutation' (namas) fits giving, sometimes disrespect; the fourth case joins with namas by rule. 'To Caṇḍikā': Caṇḍa means angry — Caṇḍā, Caṇḍī; Caṇḍa alone is Caṇḍikā the wrathful; or short-voweled, unlike long-voweled, subtle-formed, hard to reach — hence the -ka name; or Caṇḍa the fierce, His wife Caṇḍī; or She rages — Caṇḍikā. Then 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks': Kaḍi means pride; like a deer He tears, maddened by yoga — Mṛkaṇḍu; 'Mṛkaṇḍu and the rest' takes -u; He tears or crushes deer; or deer-itchy. By pṛṣodara-rule it stands. Then the fivefold etymology verse: letter-coming, letter-flipping, and two more — letter-change and loss; a root joined to its sense's excess — called fivefold word-roots. Mṛkaṇḍu's son, a man, is Mārkaṇḍeya — Śubhra and the rest take the son-affix; vowel-rise and u-loss and ḍ-to-ey changes follow. 'Spoke' means told — told his pupil the eighth Manu's birth-cause, that is. For on Brahmā's couch fourteen Manus step in turn — Swayambhuva first, then Svārociṣa, Auttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa — six gone; then Vaivasvata seventh; Sāvarṇas five, Raukyas, Bhautya — the coming ones; thirteenth Raukya, fourteenth Bhautya — fourteen Manus. To tell his pupil the eighth Manu Sāvarṇi's birth, Lord Mārkaṇḍeya begins. (Verse 1.) In simple words the grammarian's feast: every letter of 'Om salutation to Caṇḍikā' and 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks' is derived by rule — assent-sound Om, guarding-root ava, wrath-root Caṇḍa in four readings, deer-tearer Mṛkaṇḍu and his son by fivefold word-roots — then the fourteen Manus are counted in order, so the eighth Manu's tale can begin.

Bowing to holy Heramba, to teachers, to blue (Goddess?) and Sarasvatī — the Saptashatī's mantra-fire-sharing is lit up. (Verse 1, Jagaccandra's opening.) In simple words the third opener bows: holy Gaṇeśa, teachers, the dark Goddess and Sarasvatī saluted — now the Saptashatī's mantra-and-fire portions are lit up.

Tortoise-hill-ocean-king-best, wisdom-moon-king-born — holy prince Jagaccandra; served by him is Bhagīratha. (Verse 2.) In simple words the patron praised: best of tortoise-hill ocean-kings, son of wisdom-moon king — holy prince Jagaccandra, served by Bhagīratha.

Born in priest-family, wise son of Harṣadeva — by him is made this commentary, holy Jagaccandra-moonlight. (Verse 3.) In simple words the author signs: priest-born, wise Harṣadeva's son — he makes this Moonlight-of-Jagaccandra commentary.

By Govinda's grammar-fire, well-served with effort — the book is made; long-lived be the lord! (Verse 4.) In simple words: with Govinda's grammar-fire well served, the book is effort-made — long live the patron lord!
Page dust. (Verse 5 bears a Śiva-prayer.) In simple words a page number sits here; the author's Śiva-prayer verse follows around it.

Unsayable — unspeakable — is the world of earth-mid-sky, whose birth-melting-steadiness whirls; its shelter. Self veiled in goodness and the rest; I shelter in Him, Umā's shelter. (Verse 5, with old gloss.) Combined with the old gloss: unsayable — unspeakable — is the whirling of birth-melting-steadiness of the world named earth-mid-sky; its shelter. Or: unsayable are the birth-melting-steadinesses, their whirling's shelter. Or: the unsayable birth-melting-steadiness-whirl's shelter. 'Steady-above' takes -iman to stand firm. Self veiled — by goodness-passion-darkness — upādhi-robed is He; or veiled and Self both — with qualities and without, is the sense. From upa-plus-hold comes 'shelter' — Umā-Gaurī's shelter, ground, since on His half-body She stands. Such Śiva I shelter in — I stand in Your own form. 'Śri' serves serving. Then Gaṇeśa-prayer (verse 6): maker of blocked ones' unblockedness, whose memory-praises kill sins — I praise the obstacle-lifting bright God, pleased, mercy's ocean. Of bound obstacles, of unblockedness the maker — ordainer, creator. 'Ruled, bound, held' says the word-book. Sin-killing memory-praises whose — him. For sin-names 'pain, ill, misdeed' says the word-book. 'Not man-made' takes -ṭha. Pleased means content. Obstacle-lifter Him. 'Obstacle is block, bar' says the word-book. Of mercy, of pity, the ocean — Him. Shining God — Gaṇeśa is meant. I praise, I salute. Then the fourteen-verse (verse 7): 'dwelling inside the fourteen-folk, fourteen-formed; fourteen-left, Māyā-true, fourteen-teeth-bright.' Fourteen are childhood-youth-prime-age states whose — those fourteen folk — inside their hearts She dwells; fourteen-formed, form-holding. Or fourteen worlds; or in sixteen-mode, fourteen principles. Hers is that form — fourteen-formed, form-full. Or form-possessing, form-natured, nature-habited. She forms them. Or theirs the former. By graha-rule -in. For -not-end. The four and those states — by them left, ever one-formed She stands, is the sense. True indeed. 'In truth, doubly' says the word-book. Four are teeth whose — four-toothed; in him pure bright glow whose — bright-toothed. Or four-toothed and pure as crystal, like them glowing whose — such Māyā, full stop. 'Standing in vowels' takes -ka. 'State-staying many-shaped' says the word-book. At book-start, book-mid, book-end, blessing must be made, says the gloss — so at book-start, thing-pointing blessing and bow-formed blessing both were made, remembering 'blessing, bow, or thing-pointing is its face'. 'Shelter in goodness-veiled Self, Him Umā's shelter' — here lies thing-pointing; 'I praise the obstacle-lifting bright God' — bow-formed too. If blessing comes from god-thought alone, why write, you ask? To teach pupils — as teachers wrote at book-start, so must we — that is the point. 'Umā's shelter, I shelter' hints union with Umā — as Umā stands on the left limb, so may I stand on the right, is the feeling. Then the Kātyāyana-tantra verse: 'of verses seventy-eight over a hundred — five — told in the Saptashatī-hymn, by that seven-hundred count, pour with mantras — so Kātyāyana's view.' Short-e reading here is worrying — assume folk-error. We say: seven-times-hundred count, is the sense. But 'seven-hundred' as a seven-hundred group can't be — by verse-count it would be five over hundred-seventy-eight. Or seven Saptas: Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā dwell in Her — so seven-sapped She is called, and the rest falls away. 'Palatals too are dentals, plough-boar-dust' — so palatals can't be called dentals either. Nowhere is wife-word 'satī' seen palatal-first in word-books; explainers too can't call them dental. With armour-Argala-bolt-graced Saptashatī-mantra, seven-hundred pourings happen, say some — no; for even so, less-more count faults may come, and fault-hearing too. And it is told: 'fool king who pours the armour, answer by answer — his body shall fall, he'll reach hell. Andhaka the great demon, set on Durgā-fire, fell by Maheśa through armour-pouring power.' So how should Saptashatī-mantra-fire be done, doubt asks — 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks' alone, says: Mārkaṇḍeya speaks is one mantra. 'In victim-giving, -salutation at the end; in fire, fire's beloved' — says the lore. 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks, hail' is one mantra. (Verses 5–7.) In simple words three openers in one: a Śiva-prayer riddled in compounds (unsayable world-whirl's shelter, quality-veiled Self, Umā's shelter — I shelter); a Gaṇeśa-prayer (block-makers' unblocker, sin-memory-killer, pleased mercy-ocean — I praise); a fourteen-verse on the Goddess dwelling inside fourteen folks, fourteen-formed, ever-one-formed, bright-toothed; then the rule that books must bless at start-mid-end (thing-pointing plus bowing both done here — and writing teaches pupils by example); then the Kātyāyana-tantra's fire-count for the Saptashatī (by seven-hundred count pour with mantras) with warnings — armour-verses must never be fire-poured (the fool-king fell, Andhaka fell); the true fire-rule is 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks, hail' as one mantra.

Mad-maddened, mighty temple-rut-maddened sky-tuskers' cheek-joy-maddened blue-lotus-row shining — effortless, tireless, tireless-foed — may He guard from falling, Umā's son. (Verse 1, Daṃśoddhāra's Gaṇeśa-prayer.) In simple words a tongue-twister praise: shining like blue-lotus rows on the cheeks of sky-elephants rut-mad and might-mad — effortless, unwearied, foe of the weary — may Umā's son guard us from falling.

Bowing briefly to father, jewel of scholar clans — I spread the Durgā-lifting Saptashatī for the wise's joy. (Verse 2.) In simple words the fourth opener signs: bowing briefly to father, crest-jewel of learned clans — I spread the obstacle-lifting Saptashatī to delight the wise.

Here, famed Kṛṣṇa-twice-born's pupil Jaimini, hearing all duty-kind from Vyāsa's mouth, still wished to ask some left-over questions of Lord Mārkaṇḍeya — but Mārkaṇḍeya, mind sunk in holy-God-focus, had no hour — so was taught through Vindhya-hill-dwelling four birds. (Frame, with old note.) Combined with the old note: and by those birds, opening the Mārkaṇḍeya-Bhāguri dialogue, at Manu-tale-juncture telling seven Manu-ages past and the eighth Manu-age conduct — 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks' and the rest. Mṛkaṇḍu's son is Mārkaṇḍeya — Śubhra and the rest take -aṅka; 'ḍhe lop' drops the u. (Verse 1.) Combined with the Hindi program-note: first story — Brahmā seer, Mahākālī goddess, gāyatrī metre, Nandā power, blood-toothed seed, fire element, Ṛgveda form. For great-Kālī Goddess's pleasure, the use is in first-story chanting. In simple words the frame is set twice over: Jaimini, Vyāsa's pupil, still full of questions, reached Mārkaṇḍeya — who, sunk in God-focus, had no time — so taught him through four Vindhya birds; and those birds, opening the Mārkaṇḍeya-Bhāguri dialogue at the Manu-tale turn, told seven Manu-ages and began the eighth — 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks.' Mṛkaṇḍu's son is Mārkaṇḍeya, by grammar's rules. And the Hindi program-note gives first story's ritual seal: Brahmā seer, Mahākālī goddess, gāyatrī metre, Nandā power, blood-toothed seed, fire element, Ṛgveda form — for great-Kālī's pleasure in first-story chanting.

Sāvarṇi, sun's son, the Manu called eighth — hear his birth at length from speaking me. (Story verse 1.) Combined with the commentaries: Sāvarṇi — among fourteen named from self-born Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Auttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, Vaivasvata and the rest; 'at length' means with book-fullness. Caturdharī: Savarṇā is shadow — her child Sāvarṇi (Bāhvādi rule); or same-hued as elder Vaivasvata Manu — Sāvarṇi; as Viṣṇu Purāṇa says: 'shadow-name's son, the second told Manu — like his elder, same-hued, so Sāvarṇi.' Sun's-son bars Dakṣa's Sāvarṇīs. Which eighth-told Sāvarṇi — hear his birth from speaking me: 'hear' takes seeing-sense, causative-form; 'from speaking me' — fifth-for-sixth, or indeclinable, or 'from my word-spread'. Śāntanavī adds the word-roots of 'hue' and proves both name and father must be told (else any same-hued or any sun-son, like Saturn, might fit) — and 'hear' here means see-with-mind, pupil-attentive. Nāgojībhaṭṭa reads mantra-seed mysticism in it too, while Jagaccandra counts mantra-numbers: each verse a mantra, 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks' onward — verse-mantras seventeen in count. Daṃśoddhāra joins the grammar agreeing. The Hindi says simply: O Krauṣṭuki, hear at length from me the birth of sun's son Sāvarṇi, called eighth Manu. (Verse 1.)

Seeing-with-mind is meant by 'hear' — the hard-verse reading explained. (Verse 1, Nāgojī completion.) In simple words the grammarians agree: 'hear his birth' means see it with the mind's eye — pupil, look attentively.

Mantra-count: 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks' onward, this verse first of those mantra-verses; mantra number two is born — verse-formed mantras seventeen-odd in count, that many stand. (Jagaccandra's count, verse 1.) Combined with Daṃśoddhāra's agreeing grammar and the Hindi: O Krauṣṭuki, hear at length the sun-son Sāvarṇi's birth, called eighth Manu. (Verse 1.) In simple words two things together: the story-verse in plain Hindi, and the counter's note — from 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks' count seventeen-odd verse-mantras.

By great-illusion's grace, as age-lord of an age — so became the blest Sāvarṇi, sun's son. (Verse 2.) Combined with the commentaries: great-illusion — whose tool makes unlike-seeming seeming; and Her greatness is all-subjecthood — great-illusion, Lord-power; She alone deludes beings; by Her grace — 'may this be so for him' by favour-wish — as, in which manner, of an age (a Manu-age: seventy-one-plus world-ages) lord and king He became — future told as past in courtesy; and that manner, hear joined on. 'Yat-tat' pair always together. Great-shared-fortune-ful whose — blest. As Viṣṇu Purāṇa lists the six fortunes: lordship, duty, fame, fortune, wisdom, dispassion. Sun's son Sāvarṇi — repeated in marvel. Śāntanavī adds root-joys of 'illusion' and 'age-lord' (the age between seventh Manu's life-end and ninth Manu's dawn, ruled by Brahmā's appointee), and of 'blest' in four readings crowned by the six-fortune verse. Nāgojī and Daṃśoddhāra agree: past-told-as-future is courtesy (or other-ages purport); hear-joined manner follows. The Hindi: sun-son blest Sāvarṇi, by holy great-illusion's grace, as age-lord became — hear that occasion at length, know it. (Verse 2.)

Fortune-fulness verse: lordship, duty, fame, fortune, wisdom, dispassion — six are called 'fortune'; sun's son, dynasty-spreader, sun-praised. (Verse 2, fortune-list.) In simple words the famous six-fortune verse is quoted whole: total lordship, duty, fame, fortune, wisdom, dispassion — these six are 'fortune'; sun's son spreads the clan, sun-sung.

Quoted Purāṇa lines on fortune and sun-praise close the verse. (Verse 2, citation seal.) In simple words the authorities are cited and the verse is sealed: fortune sixfold, sun's son twice-named in marvel.

Jagaccandra's mantra-count (verse 3 noted) and Daṃśoddhāra's courtesy-past-tense note close the verse. (Verse 2, counters' seal.) In simple words the counters finish: past-tense for future is courtesy (or other-ages sense — apply ahead the same); mantra three, verse two.

The Hindi of verse 2: sun-son blest Sāvarṇi, by holy great-illusion's grace, as age-lord became — hear that occasion at length, know it. (Verse 2, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee repeats it plainly: by the Mother-illusion's grace the sun's blest son became age-lord — hear how, at length.

In Svārociṣa's interval before, Chaitra-clan-born — Suratha by name was king over the whole earth-disc. (Verse 3.) Combined with the commentaries: here history descends. 'In Svārociṣa's interval' — Svaroci's son Svārociṣa names the second Manu; in his rule-marked interval-time, in the second Manu-age, is the sense — Manu-age means Manu's time, says Viṣṇu Purāṇa. 'Before' means before tale-time. Chaitra, Svārociṣa Manu's son's son; in his line, community, was born whose — by name famed Suratha, is the sense. Śāntanavī piles root-proofs of Svaroci, interval, Chaitra, clan, birth and Suratha ('good-charioted'). Nāgojī, Jagaccandra and Daṃśoddhāra agree briefly. The Hindi: long ago in Svārociṣa Manu-age (second Manu), Chaitra-born, famed Suratha ruled the whole earth-disc. (Verse 3.)
Chaitra-born, famed Suratha ruled the whole earth-disc long ago in the second Manu-age. (Verse 3, Hindi.) In simple words the scene is set: second age, Chaitra line, King Suratha, whole-earth king.

Ruling rightly his folk like own bosom-born sons — his foes became kings, Kola-fort-breakers then. (Verse 4.) Combined with the commentaries: 'Kola' some call a warrior-clan; others Suratha's second capital. Caturdharī: ruling folk by policy-books like dharma-wife-born sons — his foes grew past measure. Who? Kola-fort-breakers — others' fort-city Kola, dwelling to break it is their habit (vi- makes the root mean otherwise); so Kola-dweller kings became his rivals. Or Kola is Suratha's second capital, which they habitually crush. Or then, at that time, his foes had crushed Kola. Or Kolas are pigs whom they don't crush — the Yavanas! Or Kola a weapon-kind — breaking with it is their habit, says the word-book. Śāntanavī: then, in that Svārociṣa-age time, ruling folk faultlessly like bosom-made sons — guarding from pains — his foes, harm-doers, became. Ko-Brahmā, A-Viṣṇu, U-Maheśvara — taking them for worship are Kolas, brahmins and the rest; smashing them all around are demon-wombed Kola-breakers. Or Kolas are pigs, not smashing them are pig-saving Yavanas. Or piercing pigs are Kola-piercers — 'nahi-vṛtti' lengthens; Kola-piercers are warriors and the rest; smashing them are Kola-piercer-smashers, Yavanas. And if pig-guarding Yavanas are Kola-kept, smashing them is Kola-kept-smasher — Suratha's own epithet too could be that; enough spread. Pāṭhabheda adds a variant 'and' in some books, then brahmin-proof readings. (Verse 4.) In simple words the riddle-word 'Kola-breakers' is worried seven ways — Kola clan, Kola city, pig-sparers, weapon-users, brahmin-smashers — but the story-meaning never wavers: law-ruled Suratha, ruling folk like own sons, grew strong foes named Kola-breakers.
Pig: 'pig-weapon' in the word-book. (Verse 4, dictionary seal.) In simple words the dictionary is cited and the riddle-word rests: Kola the weapon-kind — breakers with it — says the Amara-book.

Variant 'and' in some books; then brahmin-proofs. (Verse 4, Nāgojī seal.) Combined with Jagaccandra's count (verse 5 of mantras, verse 4) and Daṃśoddhāra's seven readings of Kola-breakers — pig-sparers are Yavanas; pig-piercers are piercers ('nahi' lengthens); warrior-piercer-smashers are Yavanas; Ko-Brahmā, A-Viṣṇu, U-Maheśa grasped for worship are Kolas, brahmins — smashing them all around, or else; or Kola a weapon-kind, breaking with it; or Kola Suratha's capital, breaking it; or Kāla... whose capital's breakers are dwellers by prefix-sense-change. (Verse 4.) The Hindi: ruling folk rightly like bosom sons, yet his foes called Kola-breaker kings became. (Verse 4.) In simple words seven readings, one story: whatever 'Kola' precisely names — city, clan, pigs, weapons or brahmins — righteous Suratha's foes, the Kola-breakers, rose.
Ruling folk like own sons, yet Kola-breaker king-foes rose. (Verse 4, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee keeps the story-line: righteous rule, yet foes rose.

The Hindi of verse 4 complete: ruling folk rightly like bosom sons, yet his foes called Kola-breaker kings became. (Verse 4, Hindi seal.) In simple words the Hindi retelling closes the verse: good rule, strong foes — the tale moves on.

His was battle with them, hugely staff-strong; though fewer, by them in battle the Kola-breakers conquered him. (Verse 5.) Combined with the commentaries: battle means clash; staff means elephant-horse-host, hugely strong whose — his; or duty-book-following staff among folk whose — King Suratha's; with them, the Kola-breakers, clash befell. Or over-proper punishers — though fewer, lesser-meanned, Suratha was conquered — joined with breaking; win-loss rests with gods. Śāntanavī: hugely-fine force — elephant-horse-chariot-foot-tied army — whose foes, those over-strong; punishing them is over-strong-staffed he; war befell with Kola-breaker Yavana kings; in that war King Suratha, by fewer, lesser-forced Kola-breakers, was overborne — and 'conquered' here is not 'win'-root's use. Whose? Of 'conquer in win-and-overbear, first sense actionless; rising-winning first sense, second sense action-full.' Kola-named city, capital-breaking Yavana kings, by them. Or Kola a weapon-kind, breaking with it are Kola-breakers. 'Suratha was king over the whole earth-disc' — told before — now by fate, by few even attacked, sea-edged whole-earth-circle-ness his — that is the feeling. (Verse 5.) In simple words the fall: hugely-staffed Suratha clashed with them — and fewer, lesser Kola-breakers broke him; for win and loss rest with the gods.

Whole-earth kingship told before — now by fate, by few even stormed, sea-rimmed earth-circle gone from him. (Verse 5, Nāgojī seal.) Combined with Jagaccandra's count (mantra 6, verse 5) and Daṃśoddhāra's staff-grammar (fourth-means staff against offenders; or hand is staff; though possessive-from-compound is barred, possessive-sensed -in is hinted by brevity-rule, like sprout-cutting provisions; hugely-fine force whose foes, punishing them — or 'conquered' is overborne, not 'win'-root, actionless as it is; over-filler, root-splitter, army-arrayed whose — either). (Verse 5.) The Hindi: hugely staff-ruled King Suratha warred those foes; in war, by fewer Kola-breakers, King Suratha was conquered. (Verse 5.) In simple words counters count, grammarians split staff-words seven ways — but the story stands: the fewer broke the greater.

Wishing to know the knowable, asking alone, other-desired.' King asks merchant again. (Verse 16.) In simple words the second sufferer enters: there near the hermitage the king saw one merchant — asked by him: sir, who are you, and why come to this hermitage?

Near the hermitage one merchant seen; asked: sir, who, why here? (Verse 16, Śāntanavī seal.) In simple words the grammar stages the meeting: third to sage, second to king — merchant seen; birth asked, cause asked.

Near hermitage, merchant seen; birth asked, cause asked. (Verse 16, Nāgojī seal.) Combined with Jagaccandra's count (mantra 17, verse 16), Daṃśoddhāra ('asked by him,' verse 16) and the Hindi: Mārkaṇḍeya said — O twice-born Krauṣṭuki! Near Medhas's hermitage King Suratha saw one merchant. Then asked by King Suratha, that merchant was asked thus — sir, who are you, and why come here? (Verse 16.) In simple words counters count, grammarians join asked-askings — but near hermitage, merchant seen, sir-who, why-here asked.
Near hermitage merchant seen; sir-who, why-here asked. (Verse 16, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee stages it: hermitage-near, merchant seen — sir, who are you, why come?

Why grief-struck-seeming, why ill-minded-seeming? — hearing the king's love-spoken word. (Verse 17.) Combined with the commentaries: grief means lost-loved-thinking; pain-bound mind-sinking is ill-mindedness. Grief-struck-seeming from struck-body; ill-minded-seeming from act-unsteady. So hearing, love-spoken, trust-spoken. Śāntanavī: sir, ho, why seem grief-struck, seen pained-seeming? And why seem ill-minded, mindless-seeming, watched — is the join. 'Many angers are grief, feminine.' 'Many in rites, anger.' With-grief dwelling is grief-struck. 'Ill-minded, mindless, inward-minded, says word-book.' Bad mind whose — ill-minded. 'As' likens. Autumn-cloud thin life-like. So, love-spoken, love-told, that king Suratha's word, hearing, hearing. Nāgojī: grief is loved-lost-thinking. Pain-bound mind-sinking, ill-mind ill-mindedness. Grief-struck-seeming from struck-body. Ill-minded-seeming from act-unsteady. So said. Verse plain-sensed. Trust is love. (Verse 17.) In simple words the king's gentle probe: why look grief-struck — body struck? Why look ill-minded — acts unsteady? — hearing his love-trust-spoken word.

Why grief-struck, why ill-minded — love-spoken word heard. (Verse 17, Śāntanavī seal.) In simple words the grammar proves the probe: loved-lost-thinking is grief; pain-sunk mind is ill-mind; 'as' likens thin as autumn-cloud life; love-told, heard.

Grief is loved-lost-thinking; ill-mind is pain-sunk mind; verse plain. (Verse 17, Nāgojī seal.) Combined with Jagaccandra's count (mantra 18, verse 17 — joined, mantras eighteen born, is the sense) and Daṃśoddhāra (grief is kin-lost-thinking; pain-made mind-sinking is ill-mindedness). The Hindi: why do you look grief-struck and ill-minded, that is, other-minded? (Continues: hearing the king's loving word — next.) In simple words counters count to eighteen mantras; grammarians define grief and ill-mind; Hindi asks: why grief-struck, why other-minded?
Why grief-struck, why other-minded? (Verse 17, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee asks with the king: why look grief-hit, why look mind-elsewhere?
Page dust with Guptavatī's seal. (Seal.) In simple words a page header sits here; the merchant's answer follows next.
The merchant speaks: 'I am Samādhi by name, merchant, born in rich clans.' (Verse 18.) In simple words the second sufferer names himself: Samādhi the merchant, rich-clan-born.
Page dust with Guptavatī's seal. (Seal.) In simple words a page fragment sits here; the merchant's tale continues next.

Born rich-clan, famed Samādhi, merchant by birth am I — is the join. By this 'who are you, sir' question's answer is told. 'Rich, loaded, wealthy' — 'clan in house and line.' (Verse 18, Śāntanavī seal.) Combined with Nāgojī (trust is modesty; Mārkaṇḍeya, to Suratha, seeing unsaid sage-told 'what spoke the merchant' doubt-aimed, Mārkaṇḍeya says: merchant speaks. 'Samādhi and the rest.' Verse 18), Jagaccandra's mantra-math (half-verse-formed, nineteen-odd mantras so; then after eighteen mantras, half-verse-formed mantra — two-foot-formed mantra, is the sense; so nineteen, one-less-twenty, joined nine-plus-ten mantras born, is the sense; thus: 'answered, that merchant, humbly-bowed, to king, hail' 19; merchant-saying twentyfold so; by that same count-mode, merchant-saying 'merchant speaks' telling is mantra twenty; 'merchant speaks, hail' 20; again half, says: again half-verse-formed mantra should be; thus: 'Samādhi-named merchant am I, rich-clan-born, hail' 21. Verse 18), and Pāṭhabheda's variant 'whatever word toward me' Śāntanavī-approved. (Verse 18.) In simple words counters count to twenty-one mantras, grammarians join merchant-sayings — but rich-clan-born Samādhi the merchant am I.

Trust is modesty; merchant speaks. (Verse 18, Nāgojī seal.) Combined with Jagaccandra's mantra-math to twenty-one (answered-humbly-bowed-hail 19; merchant-saying twentyfold; 'merchant speaks' telling is mantra twenty; 'merchant speaks, hail' 20; again half-verse mantra; 'Samādhi-named merchant am I, rich-clan-born, hail' 21. Verse 18), Pāṭhabheda's variant 'whatever word toward me' Śāntanavī-approved, Daṃśoddhāra's agreeing grammar, and the Hindi: humbly-bowed merchant spoke to King Suratha. The merchant said: O king, rich-clan-born, I am Samādhi-named merchant. (Verse 18.) In simple words counters count, variants noted, Hindi introduces: humbly bowed, Samādhi-named, rich-clan-born merchant — I.

By sons-wives cast, by wicked greedy ones; bereft of kin-funds; sons took my wealth. (Verse 19.) Combined with the commentaries: by sons and wives — 'and' adds kin too — cast down, scolded. By wicked is cause-holding epithet. And bereft too — not only scolded. But taking wealth, casting, driving out. So wealth-funds-sons-dear-kin bereft, to woods I came, is the join. Some say 'by wealth' modifies sons-wives — for they, my wealths, taking that wealth, me bereft, they say. Dear ones are friends. Kin are blood. Foot-following is rhetoric here. Śāntanavī: from wealth-greed, by wicked ungood sons and wives — sons' wives and cast, cast am I, is the join. By this 'why grief-struck' question's answer is told. Kin-blood bereft am I — so grief-struck am I, is the join. By wives, by sons, taken is my wealth — my wives-sons, my wealth taken, taken, is the join. By this 'why ill-minded' question's answer is told. Nāgojī: by wicked sons-wives, wealth-greed-cast, scolded — scolded, is the sense. 'And' means others too. And bereft too — by wives, by sons, taking my wealth, grasping, wealth-bereft too. Share ungiven, share-less made me. Jagaccandra counts mantra-thrice-verses (mantra 22, verse 19); Daṃśoddhāra joins: bereft means taking my wealth, casting, is the join; so wealth-and-bereft. 'Taker' or reading. Taken means grasped, is the sense. The Hindi: first of all, greed-turned-wicked own sons, own wives, sons' wives and kin cast me down, that is, scolded. (Continues: kin-wives-sons took my wealth, leaving me — next.) In simple words the merchant's wound, verse one: sons, wives, sons' wives, kin — greed-wicked — scolded and cast me; taking my wealth, leaving me fundless, kinless — to woods I came.

So wealth-funds-sons-dear-kin bereft, to woods I came. (Verse 19, Caturdharī seal.) Combined with Śāntanavī (from wealth-greed, wicked sons-wives cast me — answers 'why grief-struck'; kin-blood bereft am I — so grief-struck am I; wives-sons took my wealth — answers 'why ill-minded'), Nāgojī (wicked sons-wives greed-cast, scolded; 'and' adds others; taking wealth, wealth-bereft; share-less made), Jagaccandra's count (mantra-thrice-verses, mantra 22, verse 19), Daṃśoddhāra (bereft means wealth-taken-cast; wealth-bereft; 'taker' reading; taken means grasped), Pāṭhabheda's variant 'taken' Śāntanavī-homed, and the Hindi: first, greed-wicked own sons, wives, sons' wives, kin scolded and cast me. (Continues next.) In simple words counters count, variants noted — but cast, wealth-taken, kin-bereft, woods-come am I.

Cast, wealth-taken, kin-bereft, woods-come. (Verse 19, Śāntanavī seal.) In simple words the grammar proves the wound: greed-cast answers grief-struck; kin-lost answers grief-struck; wealth-taken answers ill-minded.

Cast by wicked, wealth-taken, share-less made. (Verse 19, Nāgojī seal.) Combined with Jagaccandra's mantra-thrice-verses (mantra 22, verse 19), Daṃśoddhāra (wealth-taken-cast, wealth-bereft; 'taker' reading; taken grasped), Pāṭhabheda's variant, and the Hindi: first, greed-wicked sons-wives-kin scolded-cast me; then kin-wives-sons, taking my wealth, left me. (Verse 19.) In simple words counters count, variants noted, Hindi mourns twice: first scolded-cast, then wealth-taken-left.

Sorrowful, woods-come, knowing not sons' weal-or-woe tale. (Verse 20.) Combined with the commentaries: so-such I — weal-or-woe-tale, lucky-unlucky news. Śāntanavī: by my trusted kin — sons-friends-wives and the rest — wealth-seized, cast, sorrowful, mind-struck, to woods I came, is the join. By this 'why come here' question's answer is told. So-such, here in woods dwelling, of sons and the rest... Nāgojī: wealth-less, trusted friends-kin cast-left, to woods I came, is the join. 'So I' and the rest. Jagaccandra counts (mantra 23, verse 20); Daṃśoddhāra joins. The Hindi: scolded by trusted kin, sorrowful, woods-come — I cannot know my sons' weal-or-woe tale. (Verse 20.) In simple words counters count — but wealth-seized, kin-cast, sorrowful, woods-come, sons'-news-unknown am I.

Wealth-seized, kin-cast, sorrowful, woods-come, sons'-news-unknown. (Verse 20, Śāntanavī seal.) In simple words the grammar proves the exile: trusted-kin wealth-seized, cast, mind-struck, woods-come — answering 'why come here'.

Scolded by trusted kin, sorrowful, woods-come — sons' weal-or-woe unknown. (Verse 20, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee sighs with the merchant: trusted ones scolded, sorrowful, forest come — children's welfare or not, I cannot know.

How are they — well-doing or ill-doing, my sons? The king speaks: by whom cast, greedy, with sons-wives and wealth — why does your mind bind love to them? (Verses 21–22.) Combined with the commentaries: 'tidings' means tale. (Verse 21.) Caturdharī details the doubt: 'what' doubts, 'whether' options — theirs, sons-wives-kin's, at home, in wives-children — weal, welfare, woe, unwelfare — now, how, of what kind? Conduct means nature. 'Sons' hints wives-kin too, learn. Śāntanavī piles proofs: tidings, tale, I know not, is the join — dwelling here, staying. 'Wife'-word masculine-only, earth-only, wife-meaning. Weal and unweal, self-natured whose — so-called. 'What-whether' split. 'What-question, disgust' — 'whether question-option.' There 'what' indeclinable too. Just-now even just-now. Here fortune-rest option by 'whether'-word hints. Just-now my sons' home something lucky now holds. Or just-now my sons' home something lucky-unlucky now holds — both I know not, is the join. Lucky or unlucky I know-not, is the sense. 'Lucky, fortune, neuter; wastes, kills pains — lucky.' Nāgojī: tidings are tale. Details it: 'what-whether' — 'what now' pair in option. Theirs, sons-wives-kin's, at home, in wives-children. (Verse 21.) Jagaccandra counts mantra-half-again (twenty-five count, is the sense): 'how are they, well-doing ill-doing my sons, hail' 25; 'king twenty-sixth then' — after twenty-five mantras, king 'king speaks' mantra — twenty-six, more-one, is the sense: 'king speaks, hail' 26; half-verse-formed mantra-pair, that is, verse's 'by whom cast' and the rest — first-half latter-half mantra-pair, two mantras stand: 'by whom cast, greedy, sons-wives and wealth, hail' 27; 'to them why your love binds mind, hail' 28. (Verse 22.) Daṃśoddhāra joins. The Hindi: how are my sons? Are my children right-doing, that is, virtuous? Or wrong-doing, that is, vicious grown? The king said: by greedy sons, wives, kin, for wealth's sake, cast aside — why does your mind bind love to them? Why is your mind's love-bond to them alone? (Verse 22.) In simple words the king's koan to the merchant: greedy kin cast you for wealth — yet why does your mind keep loving them?

Greedy kin cast you for wealth — yet why does your mind keep loving them? (Verse 22, Śāntanavī seal.) In simple words the grammar proves the koan: well-doing or ill-doing sons — how shall I know? — yet loving-them-mind binds; shameful, blameful, quitting-worthy, is the feeling; as told: 'loving in love, milking in milking again; goodness to good, badness to bad'.

Greedy-kin-cast, yet mind-loving — shameful bond. (Verse 22, Nāgojī seal.) Combined with Jagaccandra's mantra-half-again math (twenty-five; 'king speaks' twenty-six; half-verse mantra-pair twenty-seven, twenty-eight. Verse 22) and Daṃśoddhāra's joining. The Hindi: my sons, how are they — well-doing or ill-doing? The king said: by greedy sons-wives-kin, for wealth cast aside — why does your mind bind love to them alone? (Verse 22.) In simple words counters count to twenty-eight mantras; grammarians join cast-love; Hindi asks twice: sons well or ill — yet why love the casters?
Sons well or ill — yet why love the casters? (Verse 22, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee holds the koan: well-doing or ill-doing sons — yet cast by them, why love?
Mantra-half-again math to twenty-eight. (Verse 22, counters' seal.) In simple words the counters close: twenty-five, king-speaks twenty-six, half-pair twenty-seven-twenty-eight.
How are they — well-doing or ill-doing, my sons? (Verse 22, Hindi seal.) In simple words the Hindi retelling closes: how are my sons — virtuous or vicious?

The merchant speaks: as you say toward me, so it is — what shall I do? My mind binds no harshness. (Verse 23.) Combined with the commentaries: 'toward me' means toward-my-matter. My mind harshness binds not, joins not, is the join. Śāntanavī: merchant speaks. 'Whatever word toward me' in some books reads fine. By 'me'-one-word reading fits, by 'toward-me' reading the king-to-merchant humble-bowed boldness-unfit-fault falls too. O king, whatever toward-me word you speak as — this word, so indeed. Yet what shall I do — my mind, doer. Harshness, roughness binds not, does not, resorts not, is the join. 'As' holds 'like'-sense only. Gone to us, gone — toward-us-gone. Apart from us. Gone by us, known — toward-us-gone. Gone by me, known — toward-me-gone. Going-sense roots know-sense too become. (Verse 23.) In simple words the merchant's helpless truth: as you say toward me, so it is — yet what shall I do? My mind just binds no harshness.

As you say, so it is — yet my mind binds no harshness. (Verse 23, Śāntanavī seal.) In simple words the grammar proves the helplessness: toward-me-word, so indeed; yet doer-mind harshness binds not, resorts not.

Toward-me-word, so indeed; mind harshness binds not. (Verse 23, Nāgojī seal.) Combined with Jagaccandra's mantra-math again (half-verse mantra; 'Samādhi-named merchant am I, rich-clan-born, hail' 21. Verse 18), Pāṭhabheda's variant 'whatever word toward me' Śāntanavī-approved, Daṃśoddhāra's agreeing grammar, and the Hindi: the merchant said — what you said toward me stands exactly so, but what shall I do — my mind cannot bind harshness toward those wives, sons and kin. (Verse 23.) In simple words counters count, variants noted, Hindi surrenders: so it is — yet harshness my mind binds not.

What you said toward me stands exactly so — yet my mind cannot bind harshness toward them. (Verse 23, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee surrenders with the merchant: true, all true — yet harshness my mind binds not.

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: And he did so. Then, to oblige Jaimini's questions, while explaining creation and the Purāṇa-limbs, the religion-birds, keen to teach the fourth Purāṇa-limb, follow the Mārkaṇḍeya-Bhāguri dialogue-tale, opening the eighth Manu-age, and said: 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks.' Mārkaṇḍu's son is Mārkaṇḍeya — deer-tearing and the rest debated; his son is Mārkaṇḍeya. And starting the book with the long-lived one is for blessing. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Salutation to Lord Gaṇeśa.

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: …at melting time, able, mercy-formed Brahmā-Fortune Caṇḍikā. (Continues: having worshipped the first power, misery-burning, holy Tomara — Śāntanu, famed in Purāṇa glory — explains for fame. Verse 3.)

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: A full grammar-feast on 'Om salutation to Caṇḍikā' and 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks': guarding-root ava with affix-drops; Om the assent-sound heading every beginning, one-letter Brahman over all mantras; salutation-word's cases; Caṇḍa-wrath in four readings (angry, short-voweled subtle, fierce's wife, raging one); deer-tearer Mṛkaṇḍu and his -son by fivefold word-roots; spoke means told his pupil the eighth Manu's birth-cause; then the fourteen Manus counted in order — six gone, Vaivasvata seventh, Sāvarṇi five, Raukya thirteenth, Bhautya fourteenth — so Lord Mārkaṇḍeya begins the eighth Manu's tale. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 1 stands as is.

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Salutation to Lord Gaṇeśa.

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: A full grammar-feast on the Śiva-verse (unsayable world-whirl's shelter, quality-veiled Self, Umā's shelter), the Gaṇeśa-verse (block-makers' unblocker, sin-memory-killer, pleased mercy-ocean), and the fourteen-verse (fourteen-folk-dweller, fourteen-formed, ever-one-formed, bright-toothed) — then the rule that books must bless at start-mid-end (thing-pointing plus bowing both done here — and writing teaches pupils by example); then the Kātyāyana-tantra's fire-count for the Saptashatī (by seven-hundred count pour with mantras) with warnings — armour-verses must never be fire-poured (the fool-king fell, Andhaka fell); the true fire-rule is 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks, hail' as one mantra. (Verses 5–7.)

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Salutation to Lord Gaṇeśa.

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: Kṛṣṇa-twice-born's pupil Jaimini, hearing all duty-kind from Vyāsa's mouth, still wished to ask some left-over questions of Lord Mārkaṇḍeya — but Mārkaṇḍeya, mind sunk in holy-God-focus, had no hour — so was taught through Vindhya-hill-dwelling four birds. And by those birds, opening the Mārkaṇḍeya-Bhāguri dialogue, at Manu-tale-juncture telling seven Manu-ages past and the eighth Manu-age conduct — 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks' and the rest. Mṛkaṇḍu's son is Mārkaṇḍeya — Śubhra and the rest take -aṅka; 'ḍhe lop' drops the u. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Program-note for the first story: Brahmā seer, Mahākālī goddess, gāyatrī metre, Nandā power, blood-toothed seed, fire element, Ṛgveda form. For great-Kālī Goddess's pleasure, the use is in first-story chanting.

tikas.author: महामुनि
tikas.simpleEn: Mārkaṇḍeya said — (the tale begins).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Sāvarṇi' — eighth among fourteen named from self-born Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Auttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, Vaivasvata and the rest. 'At length' means with book-fullness. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: Savarṇā is shadow — her child Sāvarṇi (Bāhvādi rule); or same-hued as elder Vaivasvata Manu — Sāvarṇi; as Viṣṇu Purāṇa says: 'shadow-name's son, the second told Manu — like his elder, same-hued, so Sāvarṇi.' Sun's-son bars Dakṣa's Sāvarṇīs. Which eighth-told Sāvarṇi — hear his birth from speaking me: 'hear' takes seeing-sense, causative-form; 'from speaking me' — fifth-for-sixth, or indeclinable, or 'from my word-spread.' (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Word-roots of 'hue' (coverer, covered, described, describing, praise, letter) prove both name and father must be told — Sāvarṇi of shadow-mother, sun's son, eighth-told by Purāṇa-knowers after seventh Vaivasvata; else any same-hued or any sun-son, like Saturn, might fit. And 'hear' here means see-with-mind, pupil-attentive — 'hear' as 'see' is no misreading, proved by grammar's rules. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Sāvarṇi — shadow-Savarṇā's child. Bāhvādi and the rest. 'From speaking me' — sixth for fifth, if remainder-sense willed. Hear means know — causative form. 'Not-else diminutive-causeless' bars diminutive. Sun's-son bars Dakṣa's and the rest. Or 'ya' from eighth Manu is 'ha', its epithet sun-son. And He is fire by brilliance, there most-praised, so His seed 'ra' wins. Having that, 'ha' by pointer-sense is told. Its other epithet, Sāvarṇi: Savarṇā is three-hue-nature, Her child-like kin, hue-wording 'i'. Having that, by pointer, the last dot sits in-verse in own-form. So 'Hrīṃ' seed wins. 'His birth' — His mantra, told-goddess's birth — hear, joins. Though the opening question asked only 'which seven others shall be, O great sage, tell those Manus and their gods and the rest' — yet after Sāvarṇi-tale-telling, Mārkaṇḍeya-Purāṇa closes with 'Sāvarṇi's age well told to you; so too asked Goddess-greatness told by me' — thus dragging the question here proves opening-question-tie-mark. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Thus 'hail'-word goes with each mantra — settled. After the faultless, seventeen verse-mantras stand. Then after 'Mārkaṇḍeya speaks' mantra, 'Sāvarṇi' — this verse first of those mantra-verses. Verse-mantras seventeen-odd in count, that many stand. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Savarṇā is shadow — her child Sāvarṇi. Bāhu and the rest, figure-group and the rest. Hear means know, is the sense. 'Śamo-not-seeing' — diminutive-law of seeing-sense, causative form. 'From speaking me' — speaking is mouth. 'Gha'-sense -ka law, says -ka. From that, know, joins. Or 'from speaking me.' Fifth-for-sixth. 'Me' sense case-disguised indeclinable, or. 'Mine-ness' takes -tva like -tva-natured. Or 'from speaking me, at length' — word-spread. 'Spread is split, wide; and word's spread' — says word-book. 'Me' from mouth, or. Others say 'from speaking me, from my saying.' Said with mouth is mouth. Mouth-saying is mouth. 'Gha'-sense -ka. From that -tas. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: O Krauṣṭuki, hear at length from me the birth of sun's son Sāvarṇi, called eighth Manu. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 2 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: Great-illusion: whose tool makes unlike-seeming seeming; and Her greatness is all-subjecthood — great-illusion, Lord-power; She alone deludes beings. By Her grace — 'may this be so for him' by favour-wish — as, in which manner, of an age (a Manu-age: seventy-one-plus world-ages) lord and king He became — future told as past in courtesy; and that manner, hear joined on. 'Yat-tat' pair always together. Great-shared-fortune-ful whose — blest. As Viṣṇu Purāṇa lists the six fortunes: lordship, duty, fame, fortune, wisdom, dispassion. Sun's son Sāvarṇi — repeated in marvel. (Verse 2.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Root-joys of 'illusion' (world-enchanter, worship-worthy illusion, fortune's coming-law, great-first-illusion, Viṣṇu's illusion, favour-wish, mind-resolve, grace-gaze-given Lakṣmī, great-illusion's grace, doubt-free resolve) and 'age-lord' (the age between seventh Manu's life-end and ninth Manu's dawn, ruled by Brahmā's appointee), and of 'blest' in four readings crowned by the six-fortune verse. (Verse 2.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Great-illusion — unlike-seeming-seeming tool. And its greatness is all-subjecthood — great-illusion, Lord-power; its grace: 'may this be so.' Manu-age is seventy-one-odd-ages time. 'So' shows hear-joined manner. Fortune is fortune-group. As Viṣṇu Purāṇa says the six. 'Became' — past-told-as-future is courtesy. To show its must-be, sun's-son Sāvarṇi repeated in marvel. (Verse 2.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra three, verse two — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: 'Became' — past-pointing is courtesy. Or other-ages purport, this. So ahead too guess. (Verse 2.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Sun-son blest Sāvarṇi, by holy great-illusion's grace… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 3 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: Here history descends. 'In Svārociṣa's interval' — Svaroci's son Svārociṣa names the second Manu; in his rule-marked interval-time, in the second Manu-age, is the sense — Manu-age means Manu's time, says Viṣṇu Purāṇa. 'Before' means before tale-time. Chaitra, Svārociṣa Manu's son's son; in his line, community, was born whose — by name famed Suratha, is the sense. (Verse 3.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Mārkaṇḍeya tells, with this verse, the eighth Manu's past-birth-cause glory-deeds — first, in second-Manu-age time of old, Chaitra-born, famed Suratha ruled the whole earth-disc, was born, was, existed. Root-proofs of Svaroci, interval, Chaitra, clan, birth and Suratha ('good-charioted') follow. (Verse 3.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: In Svārociṣa-rule-marked second Manu-age. 'Before' means before tale-time. Chaitra is that Manu's own son. 'By name' means famously. (Verse 3.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra four, verse three — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: In Svārociṣa's second Manu-age. Chaitra is Svārociṣa's son. (Verse 3.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Long ago in Svārociṣa Manu-age (second Manu)… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Kola-breakers': 'Kola' some call a warrior-clan; others Suratha's second capital. (Verse 4.)

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: Ruling folk by policy-books like dharma-wife-born sons — his foes grew past measure. Who? Kola-fort-breakers — others' fort-city Kola, dwelling to break it is their habit (vi- makes the root mean otherwise); so Kola-dweller kings became his rivals. (Verse 4.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Then, in that Svārociṣa-age time, ruling folk faultlessly like bosom-made sons — guarding from pains — his foes, harm-doers, became. Ko-Brahmā, A-Viṣṇu, U-Maheśvara — taking them for worship are Kolas, brahmins and the rest. (Verse 4.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant 'and' in some books. Then brahmin-proof readings: smashing brahmins all around are demon-wombed Kola-breakers; or pig-saving Yavanas; or pig-piercers; or piercer-smashing Yavanas. (Verse 4.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Ruling rightly by policy-books. Kola is Suratha's second capital. So, past measure, Kola-breakers, is the sense. (Verse 4.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra five, verse four — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Pig-sparing Yavanas are Kola-breakers; or pig-piercers are piercers ('nahi' lengthens); warrior-piercer-smashers are Yavanas; Ko-Brahmā, A-Viṣṇu, U-Maheśa grasped for worship are Kolas, brahmins — smashing them all around, or else; or Kola a weapon-kind, breaking with it; or Kola Suratha's capital, breaking it. (Verse 4.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: At that time, ruling folk rightly like bosom sons… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 5 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: Battle means clash; staff means elephant-horse-host, hugely strong whose — his; or duty-book-following staff among folk whose — King Suratha's; with them, the Kola-breakers, clash befell. Or over-proper punishers — though fewer, lesser-meanned, Suratha was conquered — joined with breaking; win-loss rests with gods. (Verse 5.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Hugely-fine force — elephant-horse-chariot-foot-tied army — whose foes, those over-strong; punishing them is over-strong-staffed he; war befell with Kola-breaker Yavana kings; in that war King Suratha, by fewer, lesser-forced Kola-breakers, was overborne — and 'conquered' here is not 'win'-root's use. Kola-named city, capital-breaking Yavana kings, by them. (Verse 5.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Of over-strong-staff-wielding. By poetic license and the rest, this defeat-cause. With fewer, lesser-meanned. (Verse 5.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra six, verse five — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Over-strong staff against offenders is the fourth means whose. Hand is staff. Though possessive-from-compound is barred, possessive-sensed -in is hinted by brevity-rule. Hugely-fine force whose foes, punishing them — or 'conquered' is overborne, not 'win'-root, actionless as it is. (Verse 5.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Hugely staff-ruled King Suratha warred those foes… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 6 stands as is. (Page dust follows.)

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: Then after, to own city — own capital, or root-realm chief — seized, overborne, land-cut though, by them seized. (Verse 6.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Then at war-rule time, from defeat, by mighty foes seized, pervaded, scolded — the blest Suratha, come to own city, became own-land's lord — own town-district's lord alone he stayed, not world-emperor, is the join. Though foe-seized, yet by that seizure-struck forest-dwelling sage-best-told great-illusion sole-serving won-boon-earned lost-empire-regained eighth-Manuhood-future-worthiness — 'blest' stands meaningful indeed. (Verse 6.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Then, after rout. Seized by mighty foes, home-come blest — own-district lord only now, not world-emperor; keeping past-and-past-life great-kingship in mind, 'blest' is said. (Verse 6.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra seven, verse six — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Then at wartime, from overbearing-earned, sage-best-told Goddess-serving-won age-lordhood-only-fated, 'blest'. (Verse 6.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Then, seized by those mighty foes, overborne… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 7 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'His' takes every case; in his own city too, by ministers treasury seized and troops seized — is the join. Strong means strength-grown; wicked means limit-crossed; ill-souled means ill-purposed, kingdom-grab-resolved. Treasury means gold-and-eight-metals-hoard. (Verse 7.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: In that mere scorned foe-taken land-city, dwelling, strengthless, foe-land-taken, counsel-energy-zeal-void Suratha — treasury and troops by strong boundary-crossed ill-purposed kingdom-grab-resolved ministers seized, self-made. Near-dwelling ministers. Treasury is eight-metal-hoard. (Verse 7.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Then, his. In his own city, treasury-hoard and troops seized. Self-made. Wickedness is king-hate; ill-souled is throne-greed-struck; weak is force-thinned by foe-made rout. (Verse 7.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra eight, verse seven — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: By wicked lust-anger-faulted, master-betraying blamed-hearted — no repeat; neuter-singular split; 'his' takes every case; 'staying' or a reading; fifth-ending or. (Verse 7.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant 'then' in some books.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: There in his own city too, weak King Suratha's treasury and troops — royal hoard and army both — wicked, ill-souled, strong ministers took in hand. (Verse 7.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 8 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: On hunting-pretext — deer-killing-ploy — lordship-lost, mastery-gone is he; lonely, secondless; dense, impassable woods. (Verse 8.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Since ministers seized hoard-troops, lordship-lost Suratha-king, lonely, helpless, only on hunting-pretext horse-mounted, went to dense creeper-covered-belly woods — hunting-habit means deer-seeking, its ply is excuse; by hunting-trade-ploy, sage-wood-visiting itself is the main work here, not deer-doing; hiding main-work's nature is 'pretext.' (Verse 8.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Lordship-lost, mastery-gone; lonely, helpless. (Verse 8.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra nine, verse eight — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Then means after-that; lonely means helpless. (Verse 8.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Ministers seized hoard and troops… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Medhas means Sumedhas-named special sage. But in Fortune-lore: births with stories, hymns too, by Veda-speakers, told of old, O Indra, by great Vasiṣṭha — in Svārociṣa's age, to King Suratha the great-souled, and to Samādhi the merchant, bowed and sinking. Either's epithet of the other, or by age-split both names stand. (Verse 9.)

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: There — sage-dwelling-fit place, twice-best brahmin Medhas-named; calm, violence-free beasts filling; sage's pupils, thinker-pupils graced. (Verse 9.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Twice' calls; 'best' titles the king — Mārkaṇḍeya calls his pupil: O twice-born, hear Suratha's tale eagerly. He, best, fit — Suratha there in that wood, Sumedhas-named sage's pupil-graced, calm-beast-filled hermitage saw, is the join. Hermitage means penance-home. Twice-born means mother-and-cord-born. Well-famed wisdom whose — Sumedhas. By his penance-power, calm, violence-quit beasts filling. Dog-footed are foot-beasts. Boon-worthy, kingdom-regained eighth-Manuhood-worthy is best Suratha. Pupils Veda-studying graced. (Verse 9.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: There and the rest. Medhas is the sage's name — really Vasiṣṭha's other name, proved by lore-verses. Calm means hurt-free. Graced by sages and pupils, is the sense. (Verse 9.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra ten, verse nine — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: There and the rest. Medhas-named. Calm — mutual-fair-quit or hurt-free tigers and the rest filling. Graced by sage's pupils, thinker-pupils. (Verse 9.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: King Suratha saw in that wood… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 10 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Some time' takes time-track second case; 'he' joins; by that sage Medhas honoured, here-there un-fixed-place-direction. (Verse 10.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: By Sumedhas sage honoured, worshipped, Suratha in that best-sage hermitage here-there roaming, some time stayed — is the join. Time-track takes second case. (Verse 10.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Stayed — 'some time' takes time-track second. Here-there un-fixed. (Verse 10.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra eleven, verse ten — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Stayed — 'and' misordered; 'he' joins; arrived here by that sage, near — best-sage hermitage. (Verse 10.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Honoured by Medhas sage, King Suratha roamed that best-sage hermitage here-there, staying some time. (Verse 10.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 11 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Mine' wears sixth-case-disguise-unchanging; its mood is mine-ness — 'mine!' pride — by it dragged, tamed is mind-whose — his. (Verse 11.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Then at sage-seeing time, in that hermitage, mine-ness-dragged-minded Suratha thought with own mind — remembered kin, is the join. 'Mine' is case-disguise-unchanging; 'mine' mood is mine-ness, ownership-mind; by it dragged, tamed is mind-whose — he so-called. (Verse 11.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Mine' sixth-disguise-unchanging; its mood mine-ness — 'mine!' pride — by it dragged, from retreat-path dragged is mind-whose — his. By forebears means ancestors. 'Hi' fills the foot. (Verse 11.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra twelve, verse eleven — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: 'Mine' sixth-disguise-form quotes the mood-affix. (Verse 11.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Dwelling then in Medhas's hermitage, mine-ness-dragged-minded… (continues next).

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant 'mind-dragged' in some books.

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 12 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'By my kept' — ill-kept is cause-holding epithet; so the option — duly guarded or not. Duly means fit-policy. Famed chief, first. (Verse 12.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: By my kept — by ill-kept, good-kept keeper-ministers and men — duly, holding duty, from pains guarded or not — so thought Suratha, is the join. 'To own-line-come thing, duty-wealth-aims-proving, by own-line-born, rightly guard indeed by duty' — says Yama-song — fit is this king's city-thought. (Verse 12.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant 'with-chief hero elephant ever-madded' in some books.

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: By my kept — guarding-cause ill-kept. (Verse 12.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra thirteen, verse twelve — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: That famed chief, first; manly ancient; or with-chief, officer-mated is one word; 'that chief' reading famed-supreme; rope-bond cutter bond-breaker, pride-mad, is the sense. (Verse 12.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Guarded duly by my ill-kept keepers or not? And my famed ever-mad chief elephant — fallen foe-side, enjoying what? (Verse 12, Hindi.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 13 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'My' — fallen to foe-side, foe-party-ruled, won. What, how many, how-kind joys shall win — I know not. Supply-and-join. Followers are servants. Grace is joy-giving. Wealth is yearly-given gift. Foods daily-given. (Verse 13.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Enjoyed means joys — guarding, eating, pointing, pricing, feminine. 'Know' takes self-voice. Ever-always, unbroken, perpetual. Grace-fits-gifts, wage-wealth-foods, my followers. (Verse 13.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: 'My' — sway is serfdom. What, how-many, how-kind — 'I know not' joins on. Followers are servants. Servant-hood's cause: grace and the rest. Grace is joy-giving. Wealth is monthly wage. Foods daily-given, by them. (Verse 13.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra fourteen, verse thirteen — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: 'My' — grace is favour; wealth love-gift; foods wages. (Verse 13.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Foe-fallen, enjoying what? Ever-followers on my grace-wealth-foods. (Verse 13, Hindi.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: After 'serve other land-holders' some books add one verse — 'my slim-waisted wife, my most fair son; heaven-like homes, nymph-statue women.' (Verse 14.)

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Serving' means service. 'Surely' doubts. 'Misspent' — from income, fourth-part spending is right-spending; else than that, misspending; doing it, or misspending-doers. (Verse 14.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Now, mineless, lordless, they surely serve other land-holders, other kings — serving, they surely do — so thought, is the join. Pain-heaped gold-hoard by fruitless-spending natures ever-spending reaches ruin; income-no-spend grows, spend-no-income kills, matched stays former. (Verse 14.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Serving too, these alone are causes; surely doubts; alas me, add 'alas'; misspent means over-fourth-part spending is misspending; ever means all. (Verse 14.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra fifteen, verse fourteen — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: 'Misspent' separate word — this misspent, is the sense. (Verse 14.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: They today surely follow other kings. (Verse 14, Hindi.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 15 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'With pain' — pain-gone is sense whose, that pain; pain-struck, ungenerous, six-ending-verb ban rescues. 'Heaped' and the rest. (Verse 15.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: That king Suratha — this told before and else too, ever — spread palace-inside, other-palace-inside, land-inside — all his own things kept thinking, is the join. (Verse 15.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: 'With pain' — some read without visarga; visarga-loss. Hoard is root-wealth. Else unspoken too. (Verse 15.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra sixteen, verse fifteen — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Heaped and else — kingdom-lost, how kingdom-regained, spread other-palace-gone, ever-thought. (Verse 15.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Pain-heaped hoard of mine shall waste away… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 16 stands as is. (Doubled seal.)

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Twice' is Bhāguri's call, Medhas's epithet or. Near, the king saw one, secondless merchant. Merchant — asked by the king. 'Sir' calls. Here, in hermitage. (Verse 16.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Suratha there in penance-wood, thinking his own things so, near twice-sage Sumedhas-sage's hermitage-near land, saw some merchant — third to the sage, second to self, is the sense. Merchant's son, clan-born merchant. 'Saw' — some read 'saw!' (Verse 16.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: There and the rest. 'Twice' is Bhāguri's call, or hermitage-epithet meaning sage-sense. Near, close. That merchant. 'Sir' calls. Here, in hermitage. (Verse 16.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra seventeen, verse sixteen — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: 'Asked by him.' (Verse 16.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Mārkaṇḍeya said — O twice-born Krauṣṭuki! Near Medhas's hermitage King Suratha saw one merchant. (Continues: asked — sir, who, why — next.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 17 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: Lost-loved-thinking is grief. Pain-bound mind-sinking is ill-mindedness. Grief-struck-seeming from struck-body; ill-minded-seeming from act-unsteady. So hearing, love-spoken, trust-spoken. (Verse 17.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Sir, ho, why seem grief-struck, seen pained-seeming? And why seem ill-minded, mindless-seeming, watched — is the join. Grief with dwelling is grief-struck. Ill-minded, mindless, inward-minded, says word-book. Bad mind whose — ill-minded. 'As' likens. Autumn-cloud thin life-like. So, love-spoken, love-told, that king Suratha's word, hearing, hearing. (Verse 17.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Grief is loved-lost-thinking. Pain-bound mind-sinking, ill-mind ill-mindedness. Grief-struck-seeming from struck-body. Ill-minded-seeming from act-unsteady. So said. Verse plain-sensed. Trust is love. (Verse 17.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra eighteen, verse seventeen — joined, mantras eighteen born, is the sense. (Verse 17.)

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Grief is kin-lost-thinking; pain-made mind-sinking is ill-mindedness. (Verse 17.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Why do you look grief-struck and ill-minded… (continues next).

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: Answered — gave answer. Humbly-bowed, bowed from modesty. (Verse 18.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: That merchant, aiming at King Suratha, humbly-bowed, bowed with modesty, answered — is the join. To tell the answer to Suratha-made questions, he took up speech, is the feeling. Rich-clan-born, famed Samādhi-named, merchant by birth am I — is the join. By this 'who are you, sir' question's answer is told. 'Loaded, wealthy, rich' — 'clan in house and line.' (Verse 18.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Trust is modesty. Mārkaṇḍeya, to Suratha, seeing unsaid sage-told 'what spoke the merchant' doubt-aimed, Mārkaṇḍeya says: merchant speaks. 'Samādhi and the rest.' (Verse 18.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Half-verse-formed, nineteen-odd mantras so; then after eighteen mantras, half-verse-formed mantra — two-foot-formed mantra, is the sense; so nineteen, one-less-twenty, joined nine-plus-ten mantras born, is the sense. (Verse 18.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Humbly-bowed merchant spoke to King Suratha… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 19 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: By sons and wives — 'and' adds kin too — cast down, scolded. By wicked is cause-holding epithet. And bereft too — not only scolded. But taking wealth, casting, driving out. (Verse 19.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant 'taken' in Śāntanavī's home. Kicked, scolded, is the sense. (Continues next.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: From wealth-greed, by wicked ungood sons and wives — sons' wives and cast, cast am I, is the join. By this 'why grief-struck' question's answer is told. Kin-blood bereft am I — so grief-struck am I, is the join. By wives, by sons, taken is my wealth — my wives-sons, my wealth taken, taken, is the join. By this 'why ill-minded' question's answer is told. (Verse 19.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: By wicked sons-wives, wealth-greed-cast, scolded — scolded, is the sense. 'And' means others too. And bereft too — by wives, by sons, taking my wealth, grasping, wealth-bereft too. Share ungiven, share-less made me. (Verse 19.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Again mantra-thrice-verses: mantra-thrice-verses, each three mantras, that is. (Verse 19.)

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: Bereft means taking my wealth, casting, is the join; so wealth-and-bereft. 'Taker' or reading. Taken means grasped, is the sense. (Verse 19.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: First of all, greed-wicked own sons, wives, sons' wives, kin scolded-cast me. (Continues: kin-wives-sons took my wealth — next.)

tikas.author: तदनन्तर
tikas.simpleEn: Then, by kin, wives and sons, taking my wealth, I was left. (Verse 19.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 20 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: So-such I — weal-or-woe-tale, lucky-unlucky news. (Verse 20.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: By my trusted kin — sons-friends-wives and the rest — wealth-seized, cast, sorrowful, mind-struck, to woods I came, is the join. By this 'why come here' question's answer is told. (Verse 20.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Wealth-less, trusted friends-kin cast-left, to woods I came, is the join. 'So I' and the rest. (Verse 20.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra twenty-three, verse twenty — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 20 stands as is.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Scolded by trusted kin, sorrowful… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Tidings are tale. (Verse 21.)

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: Details it: 'what' doubts, 'whether' options — theirs, sons-wives-kin's, at home, in wives-children — weal, welfare, woe, unwelfare — now, how, of what kind? Conduct means nature. 'Sons' hints wives-kin too, learn. (Verse 21.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Tidings, tale, I know not, is the join — dwelling here, staying. 'Wife'-word masculine-only, earth-only, wife-meaning. Weal and unweal, self-natured whose — so-called. 'What-whether' split. (Verse 21.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Tidings are tale. Details it: 'what-whether' — 'what now' pair in option. Theirs, sons-wives-kin's, at home, in wives-children. (Verse 21.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Mantra twenty-four, verse twenty-one — counted.

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 21 stands as is.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Dwelling here, of kin and wives… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 22 stands as is.

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'By whom cast' — by wealth become-cause. 'Why' questions. Your mind binds love, attaches. (Verse 22.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: My sons, how are they now — well-doing or? Or ill-doing now — how shall I know, is the join. Well-doing or ill-doing sons — how shall I know, is the feeling. (Verse 22.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: How are they, of what kind? Conduct is dealing. 'Sons' hints. King speaks. 'By whom' — by wealth, in scolding-form casting, the cause. 'Why' questions. (Verse 22.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Half again should be: again, further, half-verse-formed mantra should be. So twenty-five count, is the sense. (Verse 22.)

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 22 stands as is.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: How are my sons? Are my children right-doing, that is, virtuous? Or wrong-doing, that is, vicious grown? The king said: by greedy sons, wives, kin, for wealth's sake, cast aside — why does your mind bind love to them alone? (Verse 22.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: No separate comment — verse 23 stands as is. (Doubled seal.)

tikas.author: Caturdharī
tikas.simpleEn: 'So' — toward-me-matter, toward-me-topic. My mind harshness binds not, joins not, is the join. (Verse 23.)

tikas.author: Śāntanavī
tikas.simpleEn: Merchant speaks. 'Whatever word toward me' in some books reads fine. By 'me'-one-word reading fits, by 'toward-me' reading the king-to-merchant humble-bowed boldness-unfit-fault falls too. O king, whatever toward-me word you speak as — this word, so indeed. Yet what shall I do — my mind, doer. Harshness, roughness binds not, does not, resorts not, is the join. (Verse 23.)

tikas.author: Nāgojībhaṭṭī
tikas.simpleEn: Merchant speaks. 'So' — toward-me-matter, toward-me-topic. (Verse 23.)

tikas.author: Jagaccandracandrikā
tikas.simpleEn: Merchant again should be: again, 'merchant speaks' mantra should be. So 'merchant speaks, hail' 20. Twenty-nine-less-thirty, joined nine-plus-ten mantras born, is the sense. (Verse 23.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant 'whatever word toward me' Śāntanavī-approved. (Continues: mantra-math to twenty-one — next.)

tikas.author: Daṃśoddhāra
tikas.simpleEn: 'So' — 'from-whom-gone' reading too. Gone-by-me, known, or. 'Toward-me-gone' reading — boldness with boldness, modesty-mood would be, says some. Really, 'of-us two' rule — oneness even, plurality fits indeed. (Verse 23.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: The merchant said — what you said toward me stands exactly so… (continues next).
